analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to disclose and sharply restrict workplace surveillance of workers, including off-duty, biometric, and union-related monitoring.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: it sat in the Senate committee on health and labor from its introduction in February 2023 until that Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers with 11 or more workers to tell workers and job applicants exactly what surveillance they conduct — what data is collected, how, and how it feeds into performance reviews or firing decisions. It would ban using surveillance to monitor union activity, whistleblowing, off-duty life, restrooms and locker rooms, and health or immigration status unrelated to the job, and would bar employers from selling workers' data. It would create a new Privacy and Technology Division inside the Labor Department to enforce these rules, give workers the right to see and correct their data, and let workers, unions, and state attorneys general sue violators. The bill got no hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants at employers with 11 or more workers, including government workers. They would gain the right to know what their employers track, see and correct their own data, be notified when a surveillance-based decision was made about them, and sue for violations with attorney's fees. Workers trying to organize unions or report legal violations would get specific protection from being identified through monitoring.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must disclose any workplace surveillance — what data is collected, how and when, where it is stored, and how it affects hiring, pay, and performance decisions — and must update workers when that changes.
Employers may not use surveillance to identify or monitor workers who form or join a labor organization, engage in protected concerted activity, or report the employer for breaking the law.

Surveillance may not monitor workers off-duty or in sensitive areas such as restrooms, locker rooms, lactation rooms, or spaces for prayer, and may not be used in ways that threaten workers' mental or physical health.
Employers must tell workers within 7 days of any work-related decision made using surveillance data, let the worker review that data, and correct inaccurate data.
Employers may not sell or license workers' data, and may only transfer it to third parties with disclosure, cybersecurity protections, and the worker's ability to opt out.

A new Privacy and Technology Division at the Labor Department would enforce the rules, backed by a private right of action with statutory damages of up to $40,000 per prohibited-surveillance violation, state attorney general suits, and invalidation of forced arbitration for these claims.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with more than 10 workers, including government employers, would bear the cost of disclosing their surveillance practices, restricting what they collect, and defending against lawsuits — and companies selling worker-monitoring technology would lose business from the bans and limits.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes real compliance costs: employers with more than 10 workers — including government agencies — would have to document and disclose every surveillance practice in plain language, respond to data requests within 7 days, and rework contracts with monitoring vendors.

The definitions are broad: 'workplace surveillance' covers any monitoring on- or off-duty through computers, phones, cameras, sensors, or wearables, and 'data' includes emails, geolocation, social media activity, and even pandemic-related health information. Critics could argue this sweeps in routine management practices such as email monitoring and productivity tracking that many businesses consider legitimate.

Enforcement relies heavily on litigation: workers and unions could sue for statutory damages up to $40,000 per violation of the surveillance ban, predispute arbitration agreements would be unenforceable for these claims, and employers could face class actions — a cost structure an honest supporter would acknowledge could be heavy for mid-sized employers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefits are substantial and concrete: knowing what is monitored, seeing the data used against them, and protection from being surveilled for union organizing or whistleblowing. The costs fall on employers and surveillance vendors, and the compliance burden and litigation exposure are real, especially for the broadest definitions — but the bill allows monitoring that is genuinely related to the job and lets workers opt out of data transfers rather than banning all data use. The scale-back cost is regulatory and borne by employers; the benefit is a new set of rights for the roughly 100-plus million people working for employers of this size.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate committee that handles labor matters, and the committee never took it up before that Congress ended, so it died there.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Casey introduced the Stop Spying Bosses Act on February 2, 2023, joined by Sens. Booker, Schatz, Fetterman, and Warren.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — the standard first step for a labor bill.
No further action is recorded: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
All sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican cosponsor joined, and the bill sat with only 5 cosponsors for its entire two-year run.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on workplace surveillance — from warehouse and delivery operations using productivity tracking to vendors selling monitoring and AI tools — are better off, because no limits or disclosure duties were ever imposed. Workers' current lack of federal protection over employer monitoring continues unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Bob Casey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor.

A fifth cosponsor (independent)
for.what_they_did: Added a cosponsorship, bringing the total to 5 (4 Democrats, 1 independent).

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 2, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never supported the bill and no Republican sponsored it; the bill never reached the Senate floor, where leaders decide what gets time.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic and independent — 5 cosponsors, all D or I — with no Republican support and no floor action in a chamber where 60 votes were typically needed to advance most bills.

industries.industry: Employers using workplace surveillance (large retailers, warehouses, delivery and gig operations)
industries.note: The bill would require them to disclose what they monitor, ban the most invasive uses, and expose them to lawsuits and statutory damages. Their interest in blocking it ran directly against workers' interest in knowing how they are tracked and judged.

Companies selling surveillance, biometric, and AI monitoring tools would face bans on core uses, restrictions on selling worker data, and contract requirements. Their revenue depends on practices the bill restricts, at workers' expense.

industries.industry: Data brokers and analytics firms receiving worker data
industries.note: The bill bars selling worker data and requires disclosure, cybersecurity protections, and worker opt-out before transfers to third parties, cutting off a market in employee data.
Unions would gain a ban on surveillance targeting organizing activity, standing to sue on workers' behalf, and guaranteed seats on the new division's advisory boards.
